strengths: Strong real-world validation on heterogeneous OXE dataset with successful cross-embodiment transfer (e.g., Tiago-Sink with unseen embodiment)
Thoughtful robotics-specific adaptations of datamodels framework: differentiable proxy metric (Eq. 4) avoiding expensive rollouts, clustering strategies, and distribution shift mitigation
Consistent improvements on MetaWorld (10% over best baseline) and significant gains on OXE (61% vs 40% best baseline)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks with well-designed baselines
Good interpretability analysis showing DataMIL selects more diverse data across datasets
Extensive reproducibility details in appendices with implementation specifics and baseline adaptations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily applies existing datamodels framework (Ilyas et al. 2022) with domain-specific engineering; lacks fundamental new insights into data selection
Computational cost substantially underexplored—paper acknowledges costs are 'several times' training cost but provides no concrete analysis, making practical applicability unclear
Proxy metric validation insufficient—Figure 2 shows results on only one task (pick-place-wall); generalization to harder tasks and different domains unvalidated
LIBERO results marginal (37.76% vs 36.4% best baseline) with large variance and no significance testing; multiple tasks underperform baselines (Mug-Pudding: 4.8% vs 10.8% STRAP)
Critical ablation studies missing on: clustering granularity, co-training ratio α, selection percentage, pre-grasp weighting; authors acknowledge lacking intuition for design choices
Real-world evaluation limited in scale: only 4 task suites, all OXE experiments use single random seeds preventing confidence intervals; dramatic failure on Mug-Mug (0.8% success) unexplained
STRAP baseline substantially underperforms compared to original paper; fairness of comparisons questioned due to evaluation protocol and architecture differences
Missing important analysis: when/why does DataMIL fail? What distinguishes top vs. bottom ranked samples? How does performance scale to larger target datasets and more diverse embodiments?

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of why heuristic data selection can fail
Solid technical adaptations of datamodels to robotics: proxy metric elegantly avoids expensive rollouts while maintaining differentiability
Comprehensive empirical validation across 60+ tasks (MetaWorld, LIBERO, OXE) showing consistent 10-20% improvements
Real-world deployment on multiple robot embodiments including cross-embodiment transfer (Tiago-Sink)
Thorough experimental analysis with detailed ablations, qualitative insights, and reproducibility details in appendices
Two scalable estimators provided (regression and metagradient-based) with principled trade-offs
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead: regression 60-70 GPU-hours, metagradient 3-5× slower than training, OXE 3-4 days on 4 A100s, limiting practical adoption despite 10-20% gains

Proxy metric validation limited: detailed comparison on single MetaWorld task (Fig. 2), extended to only 4 tasks (Fig. 11); key assumption that BC loss correlates with task success insufficiently justified

Method introduces many hyperparameters without principled guidance; paper acknowledges lacking 'strong intuitions' for selection %, cluster size, and co-training ratio; different strategies for different dataset sizes appear ad-hoc
Limited multi-task evaluation: primarily single-task experiments; Droid-Multitask covers only 3 tasks; undermines applicability to foundation models

Limited methodological novelty: core estimators from prior work (Ilyas et al. 2013, Engstrom et al. 2025); main contribution is adaptation via proxy metric, clustering, and distribution shift handling
Real-world evaluation limited to 4 tasks with single seed; no analysis of failure cases or when selection might harm performance
Baseline comparisons confounded: STRAP implementation modified for fairness; acknowledged differences in evaluation protocol and policy architecture from original papers
Distribution shift mitigation via target data inclusion lacks principled justification and is only applied to real-world settings

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem of data curation for robot learning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 60+ tasks (MetaWorld, LIBERO, real-world OXE)
Well-designed practical adaptations including proxy metric to avoid expensive rollouts
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices, hyperparameters, and baseline implementations
Consistent empirical improvements across diverse settings and embodiments
Thoughtful qualitative analysis showing which data is selected by the method
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily engineering adaptation of existing datamodels framework (Ilyas et al. 2022); regression and metagradient estimators from concurrent work
Proxy metric validation is insufficient: only tested on single task in main paper, assumed but not thoroughly validated on heterogeneous datasets with high distribution shift
Modest empirical improvements relative to computational costs: MetaWorld 10%, LIBERO 1.36% improvement with 3-5× training overhead; unclear if gains justify costs
Baseline comparison concerns: STRAP modified from original (24.72%→34.96%), Flow/BR adapted for OXE (TFDS), results differ from original papers, making fair assessment difficult
Many hyperparameters lack principled selection (cluster size, selection %, co-training ratio, state weighting); authors acknowledge 'currently lack strong intuitions'
Limited analysis of failure modes: some tasks achieve very poor performance (Mug-Mug 0.8%, Mug-Pudding 4.8%), finding that top/bottom samples look similar is underdeveloped
Statistical significance not established: improvements often within standard deviation ranges, no significance testing provided
Real-world evaluation limited to 4 main tasks on 2 embodiments; unclear if robust across broader deployment scenarios
Missing cost-benefit analysis: when do improvements justify 3-5× computational overhead compared to simpler alternatives?
Hyperparameter tuning on target distribution (pre-grasp weighting w=2, splitting target data) appears task-specific, undermining generalization

strengths: Addresses practically important problem of data selection for robot learning with clear motivation and evidence that heuristic methods fail
Thoughtful non-trivial adaptations of datamodels framework to robotics including proxy metric avoiding expensive rollouts, clustering for noise reduction, and distribution shift handling
Comprehensive experimental validation across 60+ tasks spanning MetaWorld (50), LIBERO (10), and real-world OXE experiments with strong empirical results (~10% improvement)
Rare real-world validation demonstrating cross-embodiment transfer and effectiveness on heterogeneous datasets (OXE)
Extensive ablations and qualitative analysis providing interpretability of selected data and insights into method behavior
Excellent presentation, reproducibility details, and honest discussion of limitations
Multiple strong baselines carefully implemented with consistent improvements across diverse settings
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily adapts existing datamodels [13], influence functions [42], and metagradient computation [16]; proxy metric (Eq. 5) is straightforward behavior cloning loss

Proxy metric validation limited to 1 main task (Fig. 2) plus 3 in appendix; lacks theoretical justification and analysis of when/why it might fail given paper acknowledges validation loss is 'often noisy' in robotics

Computational cost substantially higher than policy training (60-70 GPU hours for MetaWorld, 3-4 days for OXE) with no quantitative comparison to baseline methods' costs, limiting practical applicability

Multiple hyperparameters require tuning (selection %, cluster size, co-training ratio) with acknowledged lack of principled guidance; ablations limited to LIBERO-5 subset; different strategies needed for different datasets
Incomplete failure analysis—some tasks show high variance/marginal gains; limited explanation of when datamodels fail or perform competitively with simpler baselines
Multi-task evaluation limited to single setting (Droid-Multitask with 3 tasks); acknowledged that 'large-scale multi-task settings remain open'
Distribution shift mitigation is ad-hoc (data splitting); sensitivity not analyzed; LIBERO pre-grasp state weighting appears task-specific, adding hyperparameters
Linear datamodel assumption not justified; no comparison to other sophisticated data curation approaches beyond heuristics; concurrent work (CUPID) not empirically compared
